transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-08-05
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Elena Ruiz (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Acadia Platform Eng), Rajiv Menon (Acadia SRE), Lena Ortiz (Acadia Head of ML)

Summary: quick technical deep dive on observability & tracing — OpenTelemetry, token-level metrics, dashboards, and VPC/on-prem considerations.

Topics: OTEL collector, token-level counters, span attributes, KV cache hit/miss, batching effects on latency metrics, quantization signal, VPC peering for private deploy

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everybody, thanks for joining, we'll do a deep dive into our observability patterns for inference and try to make it practical — elena will lead on the tracer + metrics.
[00:15] Elena: hi all, yep, quick agenda: how we instrument token-level metrics, how spans map to requests, recommended OTEL collector config for both hosted and private, and dashboard examples — uh, feel free to interrupt.
[00:34] Maya: sounds good, we've been trying to get more granularity, currently Datadog gives us request-level latency but we don't have per-token insights which makes us blind to kv-cache behavior.
[00:50] Rajiv: yeah and our goal is to tie latency regressions to cost — p95 spikes cause cost to blow up with the autoscaler, so need to know if it's batching, cache, or model variant.
[01:07] Elena: exactly, so two parallel signals we recommend: traces for per-request timing and metrics for token-level aggregation. For traces we emit a span for the overall generate call plus optional child spans for model forward, kv-cache lookup, kv-cache update, and batching window.
[01:29] Lena: when you say kv-cache update, is that per-token or per-chunk? we do heavy streaming workloads, so per-token would be noisy.
[01:45] Elena: good question — we typically instrument cache hits/misses as counters per-request with token counts as attributes, and emit token-level histograms for token-latency if you want that granularity. for streams we aggregate per 100 tokens to limit cardinality.
[02:06] Rajiv: how do you avoid high-cardinality with token attributes? we also need model and quantization labels.
[02:18] Elena: keep model name and quantization level as limited-label metrics (e.g., model=redwood-13b, q=int8) and avoid per-prompt ids in metric labels. use attributes in spans for correlation but not as metric labels. Also use exemplar linking from histograms to traces to find sample traces for a histogram bucket.
[02:44] Maya: quick clarification: you support OpenTelem... OpenTelemtry? the collector — is it required or can we push metrics directly to prometheus/Grafana?
[02:57] Samir: you can do either. recommended path is to use an OTEL collector as a shim so you can route to multiple backends; for hosted Redwood we ingest OTEL or Prometheus metrics overTCP, but for Private/VPC we prefer collector to avoid opening ports.
[03:18] Elena: example: send traces via OTLP gRPC to our ingest endpoint and metrics either as OTLP or as Prom remote write from the collector. Private on-prem: we give a collector config that forwards to the customer prometheus or to our private ingest over an outbound connection.
[03:38] Rajiv: outbound only is important for our security team — no inbound hooks.
[03:44] Elena: we can do outbound only via a secure vpc endpoint and mTLS, KMS-backed certs. we documented that in the security packet.
[03:58] Lena: ok good. micro question on sampling: do you do head-based or tail-based sampling for traces? we care about p99 and outlier detection.
[04:12] Elena: both patterns are supported. head-based sampling at low rate is cheap; for high-value errors you can do tail-based sampling by running a local small buffer in the collector that makes a sample decision after the response. our guidance: sample at 1-5% head-based for general traffic and do 100% for error traces or for requests hitting specific conditions (e.g. kv-cache-miss heavy).
[04:40] Maya: what about token-level metrics over time — how do we compute per-model p50/p95 token-latency? do you suggest histogram buckets?
[04:53] Elena: yes histograms. emit token-duration histogram with buckets tuned for your latency (e.g., [0.5ms,1ms,2ms,5ms,10ms,20ms]) and use exemplars to link to traces. then in Grafana you can compute percentile over sliding windows and break out by model and quantization.
[05:16] Rajiv: had an issue earlier with batching windows skewing latency — sometimes small batches with 1 token cause head-latency to be high. can you detect batching-induced latency specifically?
[05:29] Elena: you can instrument a batching_span that captures batch_size and waiting_time. add batch_size as a label on the span and emit distribution metrics for waiting_time. then you can chart waiting_time vs batch_size and correlate with p95.
[05:46] Maya: ok that helps. on the KV cache side, we want to get hit-rate by prefix length — like long contexts drop the cache. do you have instrumentation for that?
[05:59] Elena: we emit cache_hit_count and cache_miss_count with attributes for prefix_bucket (e.g., <128,128-512,512+), and also emit kv_cache_eviction events as low-frequency logs that can be indexed. it's important to maintain low cardinality in the metrics.
[06:20] Rajiv: the term KV cache is sometimes transcribed as K-V, we've seen confusion in our docs — just FYI.
[06:27] Samir: ha yeah. also note quantization can change token latency distribution — we add a quantization_label metric so you can filter p95 by q-profile.
[06:38] Lena: how does quantization affect token-level metrics for us? we were thinking int4 to save cost but maybe tail latency worsens.
[06:49] Elena: in our benchmarks int8 often hits the sweet spot; int4 can increase compute variance depending on kernel quality. you'll want to run A/B by model variant and examine histogram tails and error rates.
[07:05] Maya: can you share the benchmark spreadsheet that shows token throughput and p50/p95 across quantizations and batch sizes?
[07:12] Samir: yes we'll share, that's on the action items. the sheet has throughput, per-token cpu/gpu, cost estimates, and latency histograms.
[07:21] Rajiv: regarding dashboards, can you share a Grafana dashboard that has the panels you mentioned? we use Grafana and Honeycomb for tracing.
[07:31] Elena: yes sample dashboards: 1) token-latency histogram by model+quant, 2) kv-cache hit-rate heatmap by prefix bucket, 3) batching waiting_time vs batch_size, 4) exemplar-linked slow traces panel.
[07:46] Maya: about exemplars, do exemplars require special support in our APM? we are on Grafana tempo and have prometheus remote write.
[07:58] Elena: tempo supports exemplars via OTLP and prometheus exemplar extensions; collector needs to be configured to preserve exemplar mapping. we'll provide a worked example.
[08:12] Rajiv: network considerations: for private deployments we want minimal egress. can the collector forward compressed OTLP over an S3 presigned proxy or something? our security team prefers no persistent connections.
[08:28] Elena: you can batch/flush to an internal relay that uses S3 or a secure forwarder; we typically recommend mTLS to our ingest endpoint with configurable flush intervals. for strict environments we can also accept batched logs over an SFTP-style transfer — it's slower but works for audits.
[08:50] Samir: also want to flag retention: token-level histograms are high-volume, so we recommend keeping high-resolution data for 7–14 days and aggregated rollups for 90 days.
[09:02] Maya: that aligns with our retention policies. who owns reduction of cardinality if we hit limits during the pilot?
[09:10] Elena: we'll help tune collector configs; start with a conservative set of labels and increase if you need more granularity.
[09:18] Lena: quick note: our compliance folks will want SOC2/ISO docs and details on encrypted logs and KMS — is there a package?
[09:27] Samir: yes security package, include SOC 2, data residency, KMS/HSM notes. we'll attach that in the follow-up.
[09:36] Rajiv: ok on the pilot: we want a short 2-week pilot that runs a mix of streaming and batch workloads and validates p95 < 200ms on dedicated capacity and captures token-latency histograms.
[09:50] Elena: sounds good. we'll provide step-by-step runbook: collector config, dashboard json, and a small test harness to replay traffic.
[10:00] Maya: any notes on cost instrumentation? we'd like to map tokens -> dollars per request.
[10:09] Elena: yes include token_count_per_request metric and multiply by cost-per-token from the benchmark sheet; some customers do this in a separate cost job and annotate traces with estimated cost attributes for expensive traces.
[10:24] Samir: ok let's recap and assign next steps.
[10:29] Samir: recap: Samir to send benchmark sheet and pricing model; Elena to send collector configs and dashboard json; Maya to provide VPC details and coordinate SRE; schedule pilot for week of Aug 17. action items recorded.
[10:45] Maya: thanks, that was super helpful.
[10:47] Rajiv: thanks everyone.
[10:48] Elena: thanks, we'll follow up with artifacts.

End of transcript.
